warmup.q: val audit: Sink<PaymentEvent> accepts any payment event. A function needs a Sink<CardAuthorized>. If Sink were declared interface Sink<in T> { fun accept(item: T) }, could you pass audit?
options: No: PaymentEvent is the supertype, so it can never stand in for the subtype
Yes: a sink that takes every event also takes card authorizations
warmup.why: For a consumer the arrow flips. The function will only ever pass CardAuthorized values in, and a sink of any PaymentEvent accepts all of them. in tells the compiler that T only flows in. out would be wrong: a sink doesn't produce.

sections.h: A consumer only takes values in
sections.html:
A consumer is a type whose values of T only ever go in. An audit log, a Kafka producer, a metrics counter, a Comparator, an event handler. You hand it a T, and it hands nothing typed T back.

Run the substitution test again, the other way round. Some code needs a sink for card authorizations. You hand it an audit log that accepts any payment event. Every call it can make passes a CardAuthorized, and the audit log takes every PaymentEvent, so it takes those too. Nothing can go wrong.

So for a consumer, the more general type is the one that can stand in. A Sink<PaymentEvent> can be used where a Sink<CardAuthorized> is expected. The subtype arrow flips. This is contravariance, and Kotlin declares it with in. Java writes it at each use with ? super:

Java
interface Sink<T> {
    void accept(T item);
}

static void forwardAuthorizations(List<CardAuthorized> events, Sink<? super CardAuthorized> to) { ... }

Sink<PaymentEvent> audit = e -> System.out.println("audit: " + e.getPaymentId());
forwardAuthorizations(auths, audit);           // fine: the parameter says ? super
Sink<CardAuthorized> strict = audit;           // error: Sink<PaymentEvent> cannot be converted to Sink<CardAuthorized>
Kotlin
interface Sink<in T> {
    fun accept(item: T)
}

fun forwardAuthorizations(events: List<CardAuthorized>, to: Sink<CardAuthorized>) { ... }

val audit: Sink<PaymentEvent> = AuditLog()
forwardAuthorizations(auths, audit)            // fine: Sink is declared in
val cardSink: Sink<CardAuthorized> = audit     // also fine

The other direction fails, and it should. A Sink<CardAuthorized> might be a fraud checker that reads cents. Handing it a RefundIssued through a Sink<PaymentEvent> view would break it:

error: initializer type mismatch: expected 'Sink<PaymentEvent>', actual 'Sink<CardAuthorized>'.

The position rules are the mirror image of out. In a type declared in T, T may appear in parameters, and not in return types or vals. Add fun last(): T to Sink and the compiler says type parameter 'T' is declared as 'in' but occurs in 'out' position. The reason mirrors lesson 4. Through a Sink<CardAuthorized> view of the audit log, last() would promise a CardAuthorized, and the log may be holding a RefundIssued.

The figure shows the two cases next to each other. Same element types, same "is a" arrow between them. A producer keeps the direction. A consumer reverses it.

sections.h: Comparator: one ordering for many types
sections.html:
You already use the most common consumer: a comparator. A comparator only takes values, two at a time, and returns an Int. So a comparator written for a supertype works for every subtype:

Java
Comparator<PaymentEvent> byId = Comparator.comparing(PaymentEvent::getPaymentId);

List<CardAuthorized> auths = new ArrayList<>(...);
auths.sort(byId);                                    // List<E>.sort(Comparator<? super E>)

Comparator<? super CardAuthorized> forCards = byId;  // fine
Comparator<CardAuthorized> strict = byId;            // error: Comparator<PaymentEvent> cannot be converted to Comparator<CardAuthorized>
Kotlin
val byId: Comparator<PaymentEvent> = compareBy { it.paymentId }

val auths = listOf(CardAuthorized("pay_3", 1_200), CardAuthorized("pay_1", 350))
auths.sortedWith(byId)                               // sortedWith(comparator: Comparator<in T>)

val forCards: Comparator<in CardAuthorized> = byId   // fine
val strict: Comparator<CardAuthorized> = byId        // error: expected 'Comparator<CardAuthorized>', actual 'Comparator<PaymentEvent>'

The last line surprises Kotlin developers. On the JVM, Kotlin's Comparator is java.util.Comparator, a Java interface, and Java interfaces have no declared variance. So Kotlin treats Comparator as invariant, exactly as Java does. The flexibility comes from the use site: the standard library declares sortedWith(comparator: Comparator<in T>), the Kotlin spelling of Java's ? super T.

The JDK made the same choice everywhere. List.sort, Collections.sort, Stream.sorted and the TreeMap constructor all take a Comparator<? super E>. If you write your own ranking helper and forget the projection, it accepts only a comparator of the exact element type, and the shared byPaymentId comparator that the rest of the codebase uses no longer fits.

Kotlin's own Comparable is different. It is declared interface Comparable<in T>, so the in is on the declaration. That is why lesson 2 of this track could call maxOf2 on LocalDate, which is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>: a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate> is a Comparable<LocalDate>.

The rule of thumb for your own signatures: when a parameter is a comparator, a handler, a sink or a callback that receives your values, give it in (Kotlin) or ? super (Java). The lab's highest(items: List<T>, comparator: Comparator<in T>) is the shape to copy.

sections.h: Function types: in on the left, out on the right
sections.html:
Function types are where producers and consumers meet. (P) -> R is Function1<in P, out R>: a function consumes its parameter and produces its result. So a function type is contravariant on the left of the arrow and covariant on the right:

Java
// Java's Consumer and Function are plain invariant interfaces, so say it at the use site:
Consumer<PaymentEvent> auditAll = e -> System.out.println("audit " + e.getPaymentId());
Function<PaymentEvent, String> describe = e -> "event " + e.getPaymentId();

Consumer<? super CardAuthorized> onCard = auditAll;                       // fine
Function<? super CardAuthorized, ? extends Object> label = describe;      // fine
Consumer<CardAuthorized> strict = auditAll;     // error: cannot be converted
Kotlin
val auditAll: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit = { println("audit ${it.paymentId}") }
val describe: (PaymentEvent) -> String = { "event ${it.paymentId}" }

val onCard: (CardAuthorized) -> Unit = auditAll       // fine: takes more general input
val label: (CardAuthorized) -> Any = describe         // fine: in on the left, out on the right
val tooBroad: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit = onCard         // error: expected '(PaymentEvent) -> Unit', actual '(CardAuthorized) -> Unit'

This is why the lab's Dispatcher<CardAuthorized> accepts a handler written for every PaymentEvent without any extra work.

Function types also explain the odd cases from lesson 4 of this track. Follow the value. In fun each(f: (T) -> Unit), the class calls f and hands it a T, so the T travels out of the class, even though it sits inside a parameter. In fun handler(): (T) -> Unit, the class hands a function to the caller, and the caller feeds it a T, so the T travels in. To get the same answer without tracing, give each position a sign: an out-position is +, an in-position is −. When one type sits inside another, multiply the signs. A plain parameter is −. The parameter of a function that is itself a parameter is − times −, which is +.

Member in class C<…T> Where T sits Sign Legal under out T Legal under in T
fun get(): T return + yes no
fun put(t: T) parameter − no yes
fun each(f: (T) -> Unit) parameter of a parameter − × − = + yes no
fun handler(): (T) -> Unit parameter of the result + × − = − no yes
fun putAll(xs: List<T>) List<out E> in a parameter − × + = − no yes

You won't run this table often. Use it when an error points at a callback and the intuition stops helping. The Inbox interface in the demo has three members to test it on.

sections.h: PECS is out and in with Java spelling
sections.html:
Java programmers learn variance as PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. It comes from Effective Java (Item 31), and the Kotlin docs cite it as the background for out and in. The mapping is one to one:

Role of the parameter Java Kotlin
gives you T values (producer) ? extends T out T
takes T values from you (consumer) ? super T in T
both T T

The JDK's copy method is the textbook case. src produces, dest consumes:

Java
// java.util.Collections:
// public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)

static <T> void copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) {
    for (T x : from) to.add(x);
}

copyInto(List.of(1_200, 350), numbers);       // List<Integer> into a List<Number>
copyInto(numbers, new ArrayList<Integer>());  // error: method copyInto cannot be applied to given types
Kotlin
fun <T> copyInto(from: List<T>, to: MutableList<in T>) {
    for (x in from) to.add(x)
}

copyInto(listOf(1_200, 350), numbers)         // List<Int> into a MutableList<Number>
copyInto(numbers, mutableListOf<Int>())       // error: actual type is 'MutableList<Int>', but 'MutableList<in Number>' was expected

The Kotlin version needs only one projection, on to. from is a List, which is already out, so writing List<out T> would only earn a warning that the projection is redundant.

When you design a signature, ask one question per parameter: does this parameter give me values of T, take values of T from me, or both? Give: out / ? extends. Take: in / ? super. Both: plain T. The wrong answer is rarely a compile error in your own code. It shows up later, as a caller who can't pass a perfectly good Comparator<PaymentEvent> and writes a cast to get around you.

MutableList<in T> is a use-site projection: MutableList itself is invariant, and the function asks for a write-only view of it. Lesson 6 of this track is about those.

Producer extends, consumer super: the JDK's own copy has both. */ public class PecsDemoJava { // the same shape as java.util.Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) static <T> void copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) { for (T x : from) to.add(x); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Integer> amounts = List.of(1_200, 350); List<Number> numbers = new ArrayList<>(List.of(2.5)); List<Object> anything = new ArrayList<>(List.of("EUR")); copyInto(amounts, numbers); // T = Integer, or Number: both work copyInto(amounts, anything); System.out.println("numbers = " + numbers + ", anything = " + anything); List<Number> slots = new ArrayList<>(Collections.nCopies(2, 0)); Collections.copy(slots, amounts); // the JDK version overwrites slots in place System.out.println("slots = " + slots); // Wrong move. try.expect: Both print numbers = [2.5, 1200, 350], anything = [EUR, 1200, 350], and Java also prints slots = [1200, 350] from Collections.copy. The wrong move fails with actual type is 'MutableList<Int>', but 'MutableList<in Number>' was expected (Kotlin) or method copyInto ... cannot be applied to given types (Java): a list of ints can't take the 2.5 that the source holds.

analogy: A consumer is a recycling bin. A bin labeled "any recyclables" can stand in for a bin labeled "glass only": everyone who was going to drop glass into it still can. The reverse fails: if you hand out a glass-only bin as an "any recyclables" bin, someone drops cardboard in. So the bin with the wider label is the one that substitutes, which is the flip that in describes. The analogy breaks when you take things out: a real bin can be emptied and its contents inspected, but a Sink<PaymentEvent> seen as a Sink<CardAuthorized> gives you nothing typed back. Contravariant types are for putting values in, not for reading them.
world: Consumers are everywhere on the write side of a payment service: a Kafka producer wrapper that sends PaymentEvents, an audit log, a metrics recorder, a Comparator that orders settlement lines, a Temporal activity callback, a handler registered on an event bus. Declare your own consumer interfaces in T, and one audit sink or one (PaymentEvent) -> Unit handler can be wired into every typed pipeline (Sink<CardAuthorized>, Sink<RefundIssued>) without adapters. In Java code you'll see the same contract as Consumer<? super T> and Comparator<? super T> in well-designed APIs.
mistake: The common mistake is writing a consumer parameter as plain T: fun register(handler: Comparator<CardAuthorized>) in Kotlin or void register(Consumer<CardAuthorized> handler) in Java. It compiles and works for the first caller. The second caller has a perfectly good Comparator<PaymentEvent> or Consumer<PaymentEvent> and gets a type mismatch, then writes a lambda adapter or a cast. People make the mistake because the plain type looks simpler and Kotlin's own Comparator is invariant on the JVM. The fix is to ask the PECS question for every parameter: if it only receives your values, write Comparator<in T> / Consumer<? super T>.

compare.title: A consumer, declared once in Kotlin, spelled at each use in Java

java.title: Sinks.java
java.html: import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; interface Sink<T> { // no declaration-site variance in Java void accept(T item); } class Sinks { // every consumer parameter must remember ? super static <T> void feedAll(List<? extends T> items, Sink<? super T> sink) { for (T item : items) sink.accept(item); } static <T> T highest(List<? extends T> items, Comparator<? super T> order) { T best = items.get(0); for (T item : items) if (order.compare(item, best) > 0) best = item; return best; } static <E> void subscribe(Consumer<? super E> handler) { /* store it */ } }

kotlin.title: Sinks.kt
kotlin.html: interface Sink<in T> { // say it once fun accept(item: T) } // Sink and List carry their variance, so these signatures stay plain fun <T> feedAll(items: List<T>, sink: Sink<T>) { for (item in items) sink.accept(item) } // java.util.Comparator is a Java interface: invariant, so project it here fun <T> highest(items: List<T>, order: Comparator<in T>): T { var best = items[0] for (item in items) if (order.compare(item, best) > 0) best = item return best } // function types are already Function1<in P, out R> fun <E> subscribe(handler: (E) -> Unit) { /* store it */ }

compare.note: The rule is identical: through a contravariant view you may put values in but get nothing typed back out. Java puts ? super on every consumer parameter; Kotlin puts in on the consumer's declaration once, and its function types are contravariant in their parameters out of the box. The one trap is Java interfaces used from Kotlin. Comparator, Consumer and every other Java interface have no declared variance, so Kotlin treats them as invariant and you need a use-site in (Comparator<in T>), exactly where Java needs ? super T. When Java calls Kotlin, a parameter of type Sink<PaymentEvent> shows up as Sink<? super PaymentEvent>.

worked.title: Design a dispatcher that accepts general handlers

steps.say: A payment service publishes CardAuthorized events. The fraud team writes a handler for card authorizations. The audit team writes one handler for every PaymentEvent. You want both to subscribe to the same dispatcher. Start by naming the role of each type: the event is produced by the dispatcher and consumed by the handler.
steps.code: interface PaymentEvent { val paymentId: String } data class CardAuthorized(override val paymentId: String, val cents: Long) : PaymentEvent val fraudCheck: (CardAuthorized) -> Unit = { check(it.cents) } val auditAll: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit = { log(it.paymentId) }

alt.html: interface PaymentEvent { String paymentId(); } record CardAuthorized(String paymentId, long cents) implements PaymentEvent {} Consumer<CardAuthorized> fraudCheck = e -> check(e.cents()); Consumer<PaymentEvent> auditAll = e -> log(e.paymentId());

steps.say: 1. Write the subscribe signature with the handler as a consumer of E. In Kotlin a function type already has in on its parameter, so (E) -> Unit is enough. In Java, Consumer<E> would reject the audit handler, so write Consumer<? super E>.
steps.code: class Dispatcher<E> { private val handlers = ArrayList<(E) -> Unit>() fun subscribe(handler: (E) -> Unit) { handlers.add(handler) } fun publish(event: E): Int { for (h in handlers) h(event) return handlers.size } }

alt.html: class Dispatcher<E> { private final List<Consumer<? super E>> handlers = new ArrayList<>(); void subscribe(Consumer<? super E> handler) { handlers.add(handler); } int publish(E event) { for (Consumer<? super E> h : handlers) h.accept(event); return handlers.size(); } }

steps.say: 1. Wire it up. Both handlers subscribe to a Dispatcher<CardAuthorized>. Self-check before reading on: why can't the fraud handler subscribe to a Dispatcher<PaymentEvent>? (That dispatcher may publish a RefundIssued, and fraudCheck reads cents from a CardAuthorized.)

lab.title: Consumers: a contravariant Sink, a general comparator, a dispatcher
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. The variance test says but was: "Sink<PaymentEvent>": Java sees no wildcard, because Sink is still invariant.

In Sink.kt, add in to Sink's type parameter. Then write CollectingSink: keep a private ArrayList<T>, and return a copy from items. Why can't CollectingSink itself be declared in T? (Hint: look at items.)

drill.title: Pick out or in for five parameters
drill.prompt: Close this page. For each parameter, write the Kotlin type and the Java type with the right variance: (1) source, a list you only read payments from; (2) sink, a mutable list you only add payments to; (3) order, a comparator of payments; (4) onEvent, a handler called with each payment event; (5) buffer, a mutable list you both read from and add to.

answer.html: fun process( source: List<Payment>, // 1: List is already out sink: MutableList<in Payment>, // 2: write-only view order: Comparator<in Payment>, // 3: java.util.Comparator needs a use-site in onEvent: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit, // 4: function parameters are already in buffer: MutableList<Payment> // 5: read and write: invariant ) { }

alt.title: Process.java
alt.html: static void process( List<? extends Payment> source, // 1: producer extends List<? super Payment> sink, // 2: consumer super Comparator<? super Payment> order, // 3: consumer super Consumer<? super PaymentEvent> onEvent, // 4: consumer super List<Payment> buffer) { // 5: both: no wildcard }

recap: A consumer only takes values of T in. A consumer of a supertype can stand in for a consumer of a subtype: the arrow flips. That is contravariance.
Kotlin declares it with in T. Java writes ? super T at each use.
In an in type, T may appear in parameters, not in return types or vals.
Function types are Function1<in P, out R>: a (PaymentEvent) -> Unit handler is a (CardAuthorized) -> Unit.
java.util.Comparator is invariant even in Kotlin; write Comparator<in T> in your signatures.
PECS: Producer Extends (out), Consumer Super (in). Ask of each parameter: does it give me T, take T, or both?

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "Why is a sink of PaymentEvent a subtype of a sink of CardAuthorized? That's backwards." Explain it in your own words, and say how you'd write the same idea in Java.
explain.answer: Subtyping means "can be used wherever the other is expected without anything going wrong". Code that expects a sink of card authorizations will only ever put card authorizations into it. A sink that accepts every payment event accepts those too, so it can stand in safely. The opposite substitution is unsafe: a card-only sink used as a sink of all events could be handed a refund. So for things that only take values in, the general one substitutes for the specific one, and the arrow points the other way from the element types. Kotlin declares this once with interface Sink<in T>. Java writes it at each use as Sink<? super CardAuthorized>, which is the Consumer Super half of PECS.

deeper.html:
Contravariance explains a detail of Kotlin's Comparable. It is declared public interface Comparable<in T>. So when Kotlin writes a Java signature for fun <T : Comparable<T>> max(a: T, b: T), the bound becomes <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, the same bound the JDK writes by hand in Collections.max. That is how LocalDate, a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>, gets through a bound that says Comparable<LocalDate>.

The sign rule also covers type arguments of variant classes. Inside class C<out T>, a parameter of type Comparable<T> is allowed: the parameter is −, and Comparable's in is −, so T ends up in a + position. A parameter of type MutableList<T> is not allowed in either kind of class: an invariant argument is a 0, and anything times 0 stays 0, which is neither in nor out.

C# uses the same keywords, in and out, for interfaces and delegates, which is where Kotlin borrowed them. Scala writes +T and -T, the signs from the table.

One caution for Java interop: when Java calls a Kotlin function with a parameter handler: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit, it sees Function1<? super PaymentEvent, Unit>. A Java lambda fits that type, but it must return Unit.INSTANCE. Kotlin APIs meant for Java callers often take a Java functional interface instead, or are marked fun interface.
